utterances.text: If I may, on that score, if I can just give the -- Your Honours and the Prosecution some background. Apparently the word being used is "Toboze." And I'm not a Croatian speaker as we all --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE

He alone. And I think it is important and what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then make submissions on the matter. Mr. Kehoe --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Actually, I think, Mr. President, at this particular juncture, I think it is significant as to how people that were working daily, certainly quite frequently, with President Tudjman would have interpreted that comment. And that is the question that I would put to Mr. Zuzul.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Well, that's fine, and that can be then submitted to those who will verify transcription and translation.

utterances.text: Yes. Then, are you ready to call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- who is -- no protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it will be Mr. Miomir Zuzul, if I correctly understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, can you please escort witness into the courtroom. When we are still waiting for the witness, Mr. Kehoe, D1478 the letter in the two versions --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think on that particular version, we can withdraw our submission because one is just signed, and the first one is not signed, but they are -- they are the same letters, Mr. President, so as opposed to cluttering up the record with yet another document, we can just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll vacate one, the relevant number. We'll do that later. Good morning, Mr. Zuzul, I take it. Mr. Zuzul, before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that you will be speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by the usher. May I invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I heard you speak some French words. First of all, asseyez-vous. This becomes a bit complicated for our interpreters. I asked you to be seated. Mr. Zuzul, although you used one line of French, may I take it that you want to give your testimony in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour, Mr. President, I merely wanted to thank you in French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, are you ready -- you will first be examined, Mr. Zuzul, by Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kehoe is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ambassador. Sir, can you state your name for the record and spell your last name.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: My full name is Miomir Zuzul, spelled M-i-o-m-i-r Z-u-z-u-l.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ambassador, do you recall being interviewed by members of the Defence team for General Gotovina on the 6th and 7th of May, 2009, as well as the 18th, 19th, and 20th of May, of 2009?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And do you recall signing a statement on the 20th of May of 2009?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could bring up 65 ter 1D2687, and with the Court's permission, if we could give Ambassador Zuzul hard copies of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems practical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, before you came to court today, did you have a chance to review this document that's before you?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that is a document that you signed, sir, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ambassador, during the course of our discussions yesterday, you noted that you thought it appropriate to add two items concerning your work with the OSCE to this document and that you would present it to the Trial Chamber here today. Could you do that for us?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Yes. I observed that I omitted to introduce in my -- to include in my CV two important official positions that I held and which had directly to do with peace missions outside Croatia. In 2005, I was appointed to a group of seven eminent individuals representing the international community with the aim of developing a proposal for reorganizing the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, the OSCE. I think that the reason I was chosen largely had to with my experience in the negotiations referred to in my statement. Likewise, in 2007, I was appointed special envoy to the OSCE with the task of launching an inquiry into the so-called rocket incident in Georgia. In other words, this was the commencement of the conflict between Georgia and Russia on the issue of southern Ossetia. I submitted a report to the OSCE council on the matter which the council adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The other correction that I think you've brought to our attention is in paragraph 16 of your statement concerning the regular press briefing at the White House that notes that the press briefing says 3 August 1995. And I think that you told us that that should be 2 August 1995. Is that correct, Mr. Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: That's correct. I believe it was on the 2nd of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Given those additions and corrections, Mr. Ambassador, if I asked you the same questions today that you were asked during the interviews through the course of the month of May of 2009 and that have been embodied in this statement, would you give the same answers to those questions?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we offer into evidence 65 ter 1D2687.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, we have no objections. I just wonder whether one of the other conditions of 92 ter, that it's an accurate record has been met. But ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. The first question always is does the statement reflect what you said? Second, although this is a bit broader than we find the rule itself, the second issue is whether at the time you gave your statement to the best of your knowledge in accordance with the truth. And the third is would you give the same answers if the same questions would be asked to you today? Well, the second and the third question, of course, have some overlap. But that's what we usually ask the witness, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. President. I will take care of that right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, going through this particular statement, does this statement reflect what you told members of the Gotovina Defence team during the course of these interviews?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Ambassador, just at the risk of repeating this question, to the best of your knowledge, when you were giving those answers were you giving answers in a truthful manner -- in the best way possible?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Correct. To the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And lastly, once again, would you give the same answers today as you gave to members of the Gotovina Defence team during the May 2009 interviews?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we would re-offer 1D2687. That would be 65 ter 1D2687.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1485.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1485 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President -- I'm sorry. Mr. President, I explained to the witness the summary and that this would be just a summary of his statement, and that's the purpose of informing the public of the nature of this witness's testimony. So with the Court' permission, if I could read that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ambassador Zuzul received a doctorate from the University of Zagreb in 1987 and proceeded to work as a lecturer and professor at the university level at both the University of Zagreb and University of Pittsburgh from 1987 to 1992. In approximately March of 1992, Ambassador Zuzul accepted the position of assistant minister of foreign affairs for the Republic of Croatia. In June 1992, Ambassador Zuzul became President Tudjman's national security advisor. In 1993, Ambassador Zuzul was appointed to be the ambassador and permanent representative of the Republic of Croatia at the UN office in Geneva. In that capacity, Ambassador Zuzul was constantly in contact with representatives of the international community and actively participated in negotiations for a peace deal in Bosnia and Herzegovina. On June 27th, 1994, he was appointed to be the special envoy of the president for peace negotiations with the Contact Group and other representatives of the international community. Ambassador Zuzul has testified that President Tudjman and the state political leadership gave strong support to the peace negotiations. In July 1995, Serb units, under the command of Ratko Mladic, attacked Srebrenica and other Bosnian enclaves, at the same time as the army of the Republic of Serb Krajina launched an attack from Croatian soil on the Bihac pocket. The fall of Bihac was assessed to be potentially a humanitarian and military crisis for Croatia. As a result, Ambassador Zuzul was sent to an international conference in London to seek the possibility of international or Croatian forces intervention in Bihac. Following the conference in London, Ambassador Zuzul went to Split where the Split Agreement was reached under the stewardship of the United Nations [sic] and the EU. The Split Agreement provided for greater cooperation between Croatia and the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat forces in Bosnia, and General Gotovina was appointed as the commander of the joint Croatian forces. Following the Split Agreement, General Gotovina was involved in four major military operations, Operation Summer 95, Operation Storm, Operation Maestral, and Operation Southern Move which created the conditions for peaceful negotiations and the signing of the Dayton Agreement. With respect to Operation Storm, Ambassador Zuzul testified that the decision to go ahead with the operation was not made until the evening of 3 August 1995, after the Krajina Serbs refused to accept peaceful reintegration at Geneva. Ambassador Zuzul never heard of the existence of any alleged plan to expel the Krajina Serbs. On the contrary, on numerous occasions, President Tudjman expressed that he truly respected the international warnings that in any military operation, Croatia must protect the Serb civilian population. And, Mr. President, that concludes the summary of Ambassador Zuzul's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, I would like to direct your attention to several items in your statement, and starting with paragraphs 5 and 6, where you begin to discuss the Contact Group and that you were the special envoy to the Contact Group, and in paragraph 5, you said you received that appointment on the 27th of June, 1994. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what exactly the Contact Group was, how long you remained in that position, and what did you do in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: My duty as an ambassador to the United Nations in Geneva was also to participate in negotiations and to follow the work of the conference on the former Yugoslavia. Sometime in late 1993 and early 1994, it became quite evident that the conference had found itself in a crisis, that they lacked the settlements and methods of negotiations that would stop the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. The question was not describe the background of why the Contact Group was established. The question simply was: Can you explain what exactly the Contact Group was, how long you remained in that position, and what did you do in that capacity. Could you please very much focus on the questions that are put to you. Please continue your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Contact Group was, in actual fact, a reaction to the situation that had prevailed earlier on and which was unable to find a solution. That's why perhaps I started a bit too early in my answer. It was set up at the initiative of the United States. It was an ad hoc group consisting of five states which could use their influence to the highest extent in order to bring about a solution. How efficient that approach was became evident when the war was successfully stopped - that's to say, the war between the Croats and Bosniaks - and when the Washington Agreement was signed. Thereafter, to some extent formally and actively, the work of the Contact Group consisting of five states, continued. My role was to maintain regular communications with the Contact Group, with the Contact Group member states, and to report thereon, first of all, to the president of the Republic, and also to convey the views -- the viewpoints of the Republic of Croatia, and to see to it that Croatia, through its work with the Contact Group, attains its strategic and, at the time, the most important goals, which were to stop the war and the Serb aggression and to reintegrate all the occupied areas of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before we get too far on that, I mean, the Contact Group itself, and you said it was made up of countries. What were those countries that made up the five states that were in the Contact Group?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: These were the United States of America, France, Great Britain, Germany, and Russia. Occasionally, other -- certain other countries of the European Union became involved, depending on the rotation of the Presidency of the European Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador Zuzul, you just talked about strategic goals. And I will turn your attention to the first sentence in your paragraph 6 where you mention the three basic strategic goals of the Republic of Croatia. 1, being to stop the war and prevent Serb aggression; 2, establish control within the internationally recognised borders of the Republic of Croatia; and 3, integration of Croatia into the European and Euro-Atlantic community. Now, those three goals, I mean, were they co-equal goals? Was one more important than the other? Can you just discuss those to the Trial Chamber and explain the perspective, and what the Republic of Croatia was attempting to achieve and how they were attempting to achieve it.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: From its very beginnings, or to be more precise, from the start of the Serbian -- of the Serb aggression, these three goals were, for the Republic of Croatia, as one. All the global activities of the Republic of Croatia always included all of the three goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Staying with the first goal, which was to stop the war and prevent the Serb aggression, from your -- the Republic of Croatia's perspective, what were you talking about when you wrote in your statement "prevent Serb aggression." What Serb aggression were you talking about, discussing?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Of course, I could tell you a great deal about this issue and from different angles. What I could say, in the most global of terms, in the -- in this particular context is that there existed a planned and devised aggression with the aim of occupying and permanently seizing large swathes of the territory of the Republic of Croatia, as well as an even larger territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was one and the same idea of aggression, regardless of the fact that it was implemented in the territories of two internationally recognised states. The final goal of this idea was to create the so-called Greater Serbia, or, as stated in the plans that were the basis for the aggression, to create a state which would include all the territories inhabited by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt there and if we can just move through the statement. You talk about the strategic goals and you talk about stopping the aggression. And was -- during this period of time, was there a relationship, as you moved forward here, between the diplomacy and the military and how to achieve those goals?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: The relationship existed throughout the time; otherwise, the goals could not be coordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Under the Croatian constitution in force at the time, coordination took place at the level of the president of the Republic or, that's to say the office of the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ambassador Zuzul, as we moved through this and you talked about the strategic goals and you being on the diplomatic end and then, of course, being a military component and part of the strategic goals, of course, was the reintegration of occupied land as you said. Was there a preferred path by President Tudjman to be used on how to achieve these strategic goals? Was it diplomatically, militarily? What was he interested in certainly achieving these goals with some emphasis on the occupied areas?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: I can, with full conviction, assert that President Tudjman preferred a peaceful - in other words, diplomatic - or a negotiated settlement. I heard him say that on many occasions. I heard his statement several times, and therefore I dared to quote it from memory. He would say, I would negotiate with the devil himself if that could save lives and lead to a peaceful solution. Naturally, I can also testify to the fact that all the instructions that I received from him were of such a nature that they sought a way of resolving the crisis through negotiations, as well as attaining all of the three goals. I can also testify to the fact that President Tudjman always kept in mind the fact that the war would be over some day and that Croatia would, sooner or later, have to be part of an integrated Europe or, as he would put it at the time, of the western world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, if I could ask you a question we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, may I ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have now listened for some six minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- as an answer to one simple question, where you wouldn't expect anything else than what is already in the statement. That is, that the primary focus was on reintegration through peaceful means and that military solution was not the one sought by the Croatian authorities, including President Tudjman. Now this took me approximately 30 seconds to say. Why does the Chamber has to listen to something which is meant to be in an efficient way of introducing evidence, whereas from every line, paragraph 6, paragraph 15, everywhere, let's not continue this way, because then the -- I think four hours announced will certainly be cut. I mean, it is repetitious and again, as you know, the Chamber does not mind to hear now and then for a second time, the same statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, six, seven minutes to listen to something which obviously appears in the statement, of course, not in exactly the same wording, and it is for you, therefore, yo focus your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And to interrupt the witness if he starts saying in different words exactly the same as we find already in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please keep this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Being guided by the president's admonitions, Ambassador Zuzul, if we could move this along a little quickly, maybe turn this conversation -- discussion into a bit more of a conversation where we can move through this expeditiously, I think we will cover those goals. You're talking about the diplomatic arm. You certainly were aware of the military component to the negotiations and that General Gotovina was in fact a military officer in charge of the combined HV/HVO forces after the Split Agreement, as you note in paragraph 12 of your agreement [sic]. My question for you at this point was, you know, you were at this meeting in Split on the 22nd of July. Do you know why General Gotovina was selected for this appointment? I mean, do you have an assessment of the situation as someone who was intricately involved?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zuzul, in your statement, you say that it was because he was not a former JNA officer, and that he was not involved in politics if I understood it well, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's in the proofing note, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, that's in the proofing note. Yes, yes, I apologise. I read even what you send me in the morning. Yes, so why not if that is what he said in the proofing notes, we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm trying not to lead him, judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I will help you. Mr. Zuzul, is it because he wasn't a ex-JNA officer, and was it because he was not involved in politics? Was that what made him such a good choice for the job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my impression, and when I said not in the statement but in the interview that he was chosen because he was not involved in politics, it was my impression that a person was sought who had military knowledge, military authority, but who was able to achieve a good cooperation with the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because that was precisely the idea of the Split Declaration and the Split meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let us direct our attention to July of 1995 and just talk generally about the situation in the Bihac pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can bring up on the screen D1466 which is the map of the area that had been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And as this is coming up, Mr. Ambassador, just briefly, can you just talk a little bit in your dealings with the -- President Tudjman and with the international community, I mean, were you discussing the economic effect of these -- the so-called Republic of Serb Krajina on Croatia during this period of time? And, if so, what was the subject of the discussions, economically speaking?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Well, we've discussed this. From the time when the so-called Serbian Krajina was set up, it divided Croatia de facto in two parts, or almost. Travelling from one part to another was very, very difficult, almost impossible at times, and the entire economy of Dalmatia and southern Croatia was practically brought to a standstill. It was collapsing, let alone the fact that this economy based itself, to a great extent, on tourism. That was common knowledge, and the international community was unable to respond to it with any effective mechanism.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, you were aware -- were you aware of joint military activities by the RSK and the Bosnian Serb army into the Bihac pocket in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that. We were very concerned over the possible outcomes of that situation, especially since it held the seeds of a great humanitarian catastrophe, greater, perhaps, than any one before it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: That was one thing. And second --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. You can give the second one, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: And, second, it was our evaluation that, if the Serb forces, that is to say, forces from both Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia, directly assisted by forces from Serbia, i.e., the Yugoslav army, if these forces capture Bihac, that would be a military achievement of their strategic goal, which was Greater Serbia. In that event, they would control a compact territory, all the way form the borders of Romania and Bulgaria, well into Croatian territory on the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just looking at this, just so -- D1466. You see the black line going up the railway going up from Knin to Bihac back to Banja Luka. I know it goes -- there's been testimony that goes on into Serbia. Based on your knowledge of the terrain and based on the -- the railway itself, was that significant in your discussions with the international community, as to what would occur if that railway line was taken over?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: That would have given Serb forces a relatively easy line of communication; in other words, it would have enabled them to supply any kind of arms without great difficulty. Otherwise, any communication through Bosnia and Herzegovina is much harder than by rail, and strategically speaking, that would have strengthened Serb forces militarily, both in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in the occupied territories of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, let's try to -- I think it is not the first time that we hear about the strategic importance of getting control over at least that portion of Bihac because of the railway line there. Is this a matter in dispute, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, therefore, I think apparently there's no dispute about that, and since we heard repetitious evidence now on that, there's no need to continue that or to repeat it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. At this time I would just like to show two documents, if can I bring up 1D2708, 65 ter 1D2708 which is a report from Ambassador Zuzul concerning the London meeting on the 21st of July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this one where you applied for it having be added to the 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections to neither of these documents that were added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the request to add - let me be sure about it - I think there were five, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just see how this was introduced because I ... There was a motion filed to add them to the 65 ter list, I think, with five annexes, Croatian and English text, which was filed when exactly? Because if I grant a request, I'd rather --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 4 June 2009.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The request to add, I think there were five.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five documents to the 65 ter exhibit list which was filed on the 4th of June, is granted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Just if this particular document, Mr. President, is a report from Ambassador Zuzul for his meeting with various officials of the United States government talking about Bihac. And we would offer 65 ter 1D2008 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... And in conjunction with that, Mr. President, if we could add the other one too, which is 65 ter 1D2715, which is a report of, again, Ambassador Zuzul's meeting in London with Klaus Kinkel and Ambassador Steiner of the German embassy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, numbers, if you could give me dates, because I've --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first one was 24th of July, if I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The second one you mentioned was?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The second one is undated. It is a note about the meeting that says London, 20-21 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that. No objections, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D2708 becomes Exhibit D1486. And 65 ter number 1D2715 becomes Exhibit D1487.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both are admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now after these meetings in London, if we go to paragraph 12 in your statement, you then begin to talk about the Split Agreement. And if you could just give us a very short synopsis of what the Split Agreement was intended to do and what the goals were by executing the Split Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: To put it very concisely the objective of the Split Agreement was to establish military cooperation between the Croatian army and the HVO, on one hand, and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the other hand, primarily with a view to defending Bihac and stopping the Serb aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you note in your statement in paragraph 13 that the first operation thereafter was Operation Summer 95 which commenced on the 25th of July, per paragraph 13 of your statement. Were aware at that time that General Gotovina was the operational commander conducting this operation on behalf of the combined forces?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, after -- well, approximately at the same time -- when you were in discussions here and this is the -- one point of some of those letters. When you were discussing -- going into Bihac and -- or executing the operation of Summer 95, were you in consultation with international entities such as the United States and keeping them in -- up to date as exactly what was transpiring?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: I think the best answer to that is that Ambassador Galbraith was in Split for the meeting, just as Mr. Schwartz-Schilling, whom Chancellor Kohl had qualified in the presence of President Tudjman, as his special envoy. So, of course, the international community was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... turn to another note about yours, Mr. Ambassador, 25 July 1995, and that's 65 ter 1D2709.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could bring that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this is a note, Mr. Ambassador, after your meeting with Ambassador Galbraith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, while waiting, the last answer we find every detail of that in paragraph 12, to some extent, and 13 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now what did you do in putting the question to the witness to avoid that it was just a repetition of what is already in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, we're just carrying over to the next issue which is the next line of questioning, so that's why I was moving to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... set up to that. If we can go to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if we can go to the bottom of the page on the English, the last paragraph, and it notes that: "The demarche and the conversation that we had led me to believe that the United States feels that Croatian intervention in Bihac is necessary, and that they believe the Republic of Croatia will have to intervene relatively openly and from multiple directions." Now, with regard to this, and I asked this question, Ambassador, as a foundation for additional questions as we move through Operation Storm and thereafter. In your dealings with President Tudjman, was he sensitive to a report such as this, where, if the you states had said, Don't attack, would he have taken that into consideration in making any decision to do so?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: I am certain that I would have taken that position into account in making any kind of decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, how about President Tudjman? Based on your dealings with President Tudjman, would he have taken that into account in making any decision?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: [In English] That was my answer. Interpretaiton is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] President Tudjman would have taken into account any such reports all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page which is a series of notes that were made in conjunction with this meeting, being the third page in this document. And if we go to right before -- above the specific -- it's right before the specifically. It says: "Washington has therefore instructed me to urge maximum restraint by the Croatian government forces." And as we move down into the specifically, and this is Ambassador Galbraith giving this information to you. In the second bullet point: "Ensure discipline in the troops so that civilians and POWs are treated in accordance with international law." Now when you conveyed that to the president, was it your belief that based on dealings with the president that he was, number one, conscious that the United States wanted to make sure that civilians were protected; and, number two, that he took that admonition from the United States very seriously?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: I think President Tudjman understood that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'll to offer into evidence 65 ter 1D2709.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I have no objections. But if it could be made clear what the last page is in relation to the first two pages. First two pages appear to be something Mr. Zuzul drafted and then there's an attachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understood from the testimony that these were notes by Ambassador Galbraith, apparently handed over or at least attached to the letter to be sent to President Tudjman. Is that correct, Mr. Zuzul?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is attached is the written demarche that Ambassador Galbraith handed to me as a -- the position of his government, and in diplomatic jargon I understood that is the position of the government of the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you are talking about in paragraph 13 of your statement; is that correct? And officially handed me the demarche of the US government.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand no objections, Mr. Waespi. This willing clarified, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1488.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if we move forward in your statement, Ambassador, going to paragraph 13, and going to the last line in paragraph 13, it says: "Several days after the successfully carried out military operation, 29 July 1995, Ambassador Galbraith met with Minister Susak and requested that the Republic of Croatia refrain from further military actions." And before I ask you the question, I'd like you to take a look a portion of Ambassador Galbraith's diary, that would be P458. And I believe this is for the entry of July the 29th - this is only in English, Mr. President - and it would be page 17 at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can blow up towards the bottom, we're going to go just to the bottom two paragraphs on -- the entry of 29 at the bottom and -- yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Starting this with the second paragraph, Mr. Ambassador: "I received a demarche instruction to see Tudjman or the highest available government of Croatia official to press our point that Croatia should withhold on military action. This represented a slight change from our earlier position that any Croatian action should be limited." "Susak is the only senior government of Croatia official in town, and I called on him at 11.30. He was exhausted but pleased with the recent successes. He listened as I read out our points and then" -- If you can turn the page on that, please, go to the top. "That the RSK troops appear to be pulling out of Bihac. I jumped in, pointing out that the HVO/HV offensive had achieved its results, and therefore was no longer a reason for immediate HV action into Krajina. He replied" - he being Susak - "if we stop, then what? They will be back to attacking in two weeks. He provided some other military details." Now, this discussion, Mr. Ambassador, I mean, were you aware of this discussion, or did you become aware of this discussion, and what can you tell the Trial Chamber about this dialogue between Ambassador Galbraith and Minister Susak and what happened thereafter?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: I first learned of these details during proofing. I'm talking about details, I had never seen the demarche that Ambassador Galbraith referred to, and I never knew that he submitted it to the Republic of Croatia in the form of demarche. If he had intended it for Minister Susak, he would not have handed it to the minister of defence. What I do know from that time is that I was invited by President Tudjman who told me that there existed certain unclear communications with the United States, referring, I suppose, to this conversation between Minister Susak and Ambassador Galbraith. President Tudjman asked me to travel to Washington and have direct talks with the State Department, to find out the real meaning of these communications and the position of the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, in paragraph 14 of your statement you note that you did in fact go to Washington.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we could bring up on the screen 65 ter 1D1445 which is a note of your meeting with, on the 31st of July, with Ambassador Holbrooke, Ambassador Frasure, and Ambassador Hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you have seen this note before, Mr. Ambassador, reflecting your meeting with those individuals?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now if we could go to -- that first paragraph is beginning: "At the beginning."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could scroll up on that, Mr. Registrar. I'm interested in the last sentence in that paragraph, beginning with "therefore." I'm not certain if that is exactly -- is consistent with the Croatian. It's on the same page. Do you see that sentence "therefore ..."? It then says: "Therefore the Republic of Croatia is continuing its efforts to make their military successes and military initiative a trump card for negotiations with the aim of, if possible, primarily the peaceful reintegration of all occupied area of the Republic of Croatia." Do you see that, Mr. Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, even after Operation Summer 95, had President Tudjman and the Republic of Croatia given up on the possibility of peaceful reintegration of the occupied areas of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: No. At no point was the idea of peaceful reintegration of the occupied territories given up on. And if you allow me to add, everywhere, and at all times when we discussed occupied territories, we always had in mind there was another occupied territory of the Republic of Croatia, namely, Eastern Slavonia and Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let us just begin to talk about that just briefly, and we will come back to that at the end. Was -- were the negotiations concerning Eastern Slavonia and Baranja significant to President Tudjman as well as the reintegration of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Both were of equal significance to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when we talk about significance, did he, based on your conversations with him, want to peacefully reintegrate all of those lands back into the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that's leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi. It seems it is. However, not a question came into my mind what's -- especially the reason that you object against leading, where it seems that here, again, it's to some extent repetitious, and to some extent it transpires from the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, then it's a repetition of the statement and irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You don't have to adapt your reasons for objecting to my questions. Mr. Kehoe --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... I can just move on to the next topic. We will get back to some of those discussions as we go through these documents, and I can just withdraw the question and just move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I can't say that you have taken fully away my concern about the way in which time is used. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now if we can turn to page 2 of this document. And if we go to the second paragraph beginning with: "In connection." Actually it's the first full paragraph, yes. And in that -- we need to change the page in the B/C/S, please. In that paragraph, it notes: "In connection with Stoltenberg and Mr. Akashi's initiative for future [sic] negotiations with the Croatian Serbs from the occupied territories, Ambassador Zuzul just now while emphasizing Croatia's past willingness for negotiations at any given time, expressed his doubts regarding his sincerity for the wishes of constructive talks and stating that this may be an attempt to stall the situation and win more time." What are you talking about there, sir, I mean, what is your perspective when you were saying this during the course of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: As far as I can remember now, it was my impression that all at once the Serb side sent out a signal that it was now ready to negotiate in a way in which it had not been hitherto. Our assessment was that the signal did not mean that they wanted to approach the negotiations seriously. Rather, that they merely wanted to prevent their military position from weakening any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page in this document which is the last page. And in the first full paragraph it's his discussion with regard to Ambassador Holbrooke's requests. And without reading the entire matter, Mr. Ambassador, when you finished these meetings with Ambassador Holbrooke could you tell us, in plain terms, what was your take-away from this meeting as to what the position of the United States was concerning any future military action.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: At risk of repeating myself, I can tell you that on the basis of this meeting as well as on the basis of a number of other informal and formal meetings that I had in Washington at the time, I arrived at the conclusion that the United States of America fully understood that without Croatian intervention, there would ensue a humanitarian tragedy in the area of Bihac. I understood that they knew that the joint action of the Croatian and Bosnian forces were very successful in their military actions and that these successful military actions could first lead to a breakdown in the Serb military force and, secondly, in the strengthening of the Federation of the Croats and Bosniaks which is what they pointed out on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: However, by the same token --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sorry, if can I correct this. Specifically towards the potential offensive into the Krajina and Operation Storm. I mean, based on these meetings with him - with Ambassador Holbrooke and others, what was your sense as to what the position of the United States was on future military actions to retake the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: I believe that the position was as follows. Regardless of the course the military actions might take, and it was never specifically stated what course it was that they should not take, that they had to take care of the international forces that were present in the area and to make sure that they protect the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we go to -- just one last question on this document, Mr. President. And I know we're a little bit over time, just to move through this. If we go to the bottom of the page and point 4, Where you note that: "They recognised that the initiated operations are leading toward a final solution, and they, themselves, warned not to fall for the attempts to use the negotiations as an excuse in order to prevent their realisation."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you elaborate on that just briefly. I mean, what was your sense as to what Ambassador Holbrooke and others were telling you concerning the delaying the negotiations as an excuse to prevent the realisation of any completed military action? What was your sense of this, sir, that you were trying to deliver to President Tudjman and others?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: My impression over all was that, on the one hand, we should never give up on the idea to resolve the problem through negotiations; and on the other, in a situation where there was a chance to solve the problems in actual terms through a military victory over the Serb forces, any sort of pretense at negotiations which would only place obstacles in the way of a military activity could only prove to be counterproductive in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry, did you finish your answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zuzul, we will have a break --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all there in the transcript already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zuzul, we'll have a break, and we have to deal with another procedural matter totally unrelated to your testimony which has to be done in private session, so I will ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We briefly, very briefly, go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The issue of the two documents D1478 and D637, which I just touched upon before the witness entered the courtroom, D1478, that number, will be vacated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was -- the difference with D637 was that D637 had a cover page and apparently was an unsigned telefax copy of the letter. And I take it, Mr. Waespi, that there's no dispute about a signed letter which, apparently, was sent, because that's what the cover page of the telefax copy says, sent on that day, that it was sent and that it was signed. Under those circumstances, we leave it to D637. We will resume at ten minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, the Chamber has considered the way in which the examination proceeds, and considers in view of many factors, such as repetitious to the statement, repetitious to other evidence, how focussed the questions are, well, many of these what is foreground and what is details of background, that you should finish the testimony of this witness today. You claimed four hours. We take three and a half effective hours apart from procedural matters on an average day, and the Chamber considered that even with this decision, it -- that there's still a bit of again generosity in it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If can just put my comment on the record, so we can -- for future review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will attempt in all possibilities to finish in this time. I will note for the record, Mr. President, not once during the Prosecution's case did such an instruction come from you, Mr. President, to the OTP. As can you see I am attempting to move this along, interrupting the witness pursuant to Your Honours' instructions and trying to get to the core of this as quickly as possible. I have -- the Defence has no desire to make this any more lengthy than we think is to get this information is concerned. And on a pure fairness issue, Your Honour, I will point out, Mr. President, that not once did such an instruction -- was any cutting of time given to the Prosecution. If I can, at this time, move ahead and move into evidence 65 ter 1D445, which was the 31st July 1995 note from Mr. Zuzul concerning the meeting in Washington.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter number 1D1445 becomes Exhibit D1489.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ambassador Zuzul, if I may, if we could pick up the pace as you heard the instruction coming from the President. My time is now limited, if we could pick up the pace in our comments, I think it would expedite matter, number one. Number two, you need not worry about the translation and wait for the translation before you begin your response, translators are in fact having a difficult time because it is moving to slowly. So if we could move things along a bit more quickly, we could finish through this, and I can abide by the order that I have just been given to the Trial Chamber. Okay, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 16 of your statement you note the three conditions in Washington. If military actions were going to continue and first - and this is the middle of 16 - first that the operation had to be carried out quickly. Second, during the operation, maximum care must be taken of the safety and human rights of the civilians in the occupied area, and third guarantee the safety of UN. And you also note that the White House spokesperson conveyed these statements in a press briefing. And I will turn to 65 ter 1D2631. If we could just go to page 1 first and then we go to the second page, I just want to show you the initial briefing, and this goes to the correction that you made to the statement. This is only in English, Mr. President, as we can see from -- it's not up yet. As we can see this is a date of the 3rd for a press briefing of the 2nd by Mr. McCurry, the press office of the White House. And if we can turn to page 2 of this document, towards the bottom of the page, we can note the areas that of discussion - and it is the second-to-last paragraph - talking about the discussions with Croatian officials. And -- Is that the particular comment you were referring to in your statement, Ambassador Zuzul?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'd like to offer into evidence 65 ter 1D2631.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1490.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ambassador Zuzul, I'd like to direct your attention a paragraph 20 of your statement. In the first line of that statement, you note that the final decision on launching the military operation for liberation was brought on the VONS session on 3 August 1995. We have heard testimony that VONS is the Defence and national security council that was established within the government, and we've heard some testimony on that before. Now if I can ask you some preliminaries. Prior to this discussion, were you aware there were in fact military meetings prior to this VONS meeting, were plans had been made militarily for the liberation of the so-called Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: I can't say that I knew of these meetings in any precise terms, but it was only logical and an expected matter that they would be held and that preparations would be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, with those preparations that you just referred but don't know the specifics, explain to the Trial Chamber why you have concluded in your statement that the final decision on the launching of Operation Storm was made at this VONS meeting on the 3rd.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: I would like to point out that the VONS was not an ad hoc body. Rather, under the then constitution of the Republic of Croatia, which defined the state as a semi-presidential state, VONS was the body where decisions were made that were of strategic importance and related to various levels of the state. This was not the first and certainly not the last case of the sort. There were many other such cases where that type of decisions were taken by VONS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador Zuzul, were you aware of the talks going on in Geneva that were taking place just prior or in conjunction, at the same time as this VONS meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: I was aware of that. Negotiations took place before the VONS meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to talk you just briefly about the international acceptance or the international importance of the international community accepting any military operation such as Operation Storm. When you were in Washington -- and this is based on your experience as a diplomat these many years, Ambassador Zuzul, and dealing with President Tudjman. If Washington had told you -- or officials in Washington had told you during that trip not to proceed with Operation Storm, do you believe that Operation Storm would have gone forward?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: My opinion is that the -- had the response from Washington been to abort the operation, President Tudjman would have aborted it at the time. I base this opinion of mine not only on the experience from my work, my dealings with President Tudjman but on a number of similar cases as well. Let me give you the most evident example, where President Tudjman, who was not only a statesman and politician but also a general, aborted a military operation that was carried out in direction of Banja Luka which was a very difficult situation for him, because he believed that the arrival of the Croatian and Bosniak forces in Banja Luka would constitute a complete breakdown of the Serb army. As a general, of course, he wanted to defeat the other side. However, despite that, and solely with the purpose of sending a clear -- because a clear message was sent from the United States that the operation should be aborted, he did abort the operation. This is one of the reasons why I feel so certain in my conclusion that reports -- had the reports from Washington and other countries been such that they required the operation to be halted, President Tudjman would have been done so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, you spoke to us about several conditions, and it is -- what we're talking about are the conditions that are set forth in your statement in paragraph 16 about conditions under which Operation Storm would proceed. Based on your dealings with President Tudjman over these years, as a diplomat -- and as a diplomat, would President Tudjman have authorised Operation Storm to proceed in a manner that violated the conditions that had been set out by the officials in Washington? And by that I include taking care of civilians and the other conditions that were set forth.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: I don't think that President Tudjman would order anything of the sort or allow it, for that matter. If you will allow me to briefly comment on this. I knew President Tudjman very well, and I knew that he was, of course, very familiar with the terms being used in the former socialist system which were used in a different way. I know that President Tudjman himself sometimes had his suspicions of the concepts of the western world such as human rights, freedom of the press and the like. However, as a strategic statesman, President Tudjman knew very well what sort of significance Croatia's relations with other countries had. And he, despite his own character, which had been formed the way it had been formed, did not understand fully the terms as they were meant by other countries. He would never have done anything that would be contrary to the positions of other countries, especially those of the United States of America.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention back again to the 3rd of August, and this is a meeting with Ambassador Galbraith prior to the VONS meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I can bring up P458. And this would be page 25 in the English, and it is the insertion on that date, second paragraph for August the 3rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in that second paragraph, Mr. Ambassador, it notes a discussion about a meeting with -- ultimately a meeting going through there with President Tudjman. It goes to the other page. And you in fact came into that meeting, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: That's right. I attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in this particular discussion, they talk about -- it speaks for itself, but Ambassador Galbraith asking for some guidance coming from Secretary Tarnoff, you can see in the middle of the page: "I called the department to seek a stronger statement. I specifically -- I urge that we warn the Croatians that a military solution now in lieu of waiting to see if Babic delivered within a week would harm our bilateral relationship." And he says: "I spoke to Tarnoff." In then in fact at the bottom of the that page we see what he was authorised to say. Nevertheless, if we can turn our attention to P448 which is a tape of that item. And I want to focus on this issue of harming our bilateral relations. If we could bring this up, and I first turn to page 3 in the English of this. That is at P448.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page in the English. I will point out to you, Mr. President, and it -- obviously, it speaks for itself. In 448, page 24, that what is he asking for, military option, urge that we warn that a military option -- that military solution now in lieu of waiting to see if Babic delivered within a week could cause harm -- would harm our bilateral relationship." Your Honours can read what the rest of it is. But what he was authorised to by Secretary Hill, did not include any comment that any such operation would hurt bilateral relationships, but it speaks for itself. I'm sorry. I was just told by -- this is it P458, page 25. Turning our attention to the transcript itself is P448, and you can see at the bottom of that page -- excuse me, right before the president, Ambassador Galbraith says in the last sentence: "I have to tell you, since have I spoken with people in Washington, that in light of the recent developments, if this is process is not given a fair chance, if military action ensues in the days to follow without giving this a chance, then this could significantly and adversely affect our relationships."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ambassador, you were present when you heard that comment, and I would like to turn your attention to -- we -- we have discussed this with the Prosecutor, Mr. President, concerning the balance of the transcript which ends of saying, by Mr. Galbraith: "It is it true that the beginning of operation is set to tomorrow." President Tudjman says: "Yes, if the Geneva talks fail." Peter Galbraith: "Thank you, Mr. President." And it goes on yet further -- and if I might have one second as to the what the number is here. I want to bring up on screen the 65 ter 1D2719 which is, Ambassador, the balance of this particular conversation where you make some comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time if I could play 65 ter 1D2719. And a transcript has been given to the booths. And we're going to do this via sanction, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Tudjman's Interpreter: Well, you see, Belgrade is invoking in his assembly. Milosevic says he is controlling -- "Tudjman: No, Babic is invoking ... "Tudjman's Interpreter: Babic, I'm sorry, is invoking his assembly. Milosevic says he is controlling the generals. And yet he would not receive Babic and talk to him. Belgrade has appointed Mrksic for the commanding officer in Knin, and yet they are sending Novakovic down to Geneva. And all this again goes to show that we have been, again, led on. Moreover as Mr. Sarinic just stated, one of the members of that delegation is Prijic who is the grey eminence of Martic. "Galbraith: I understand the dilemma, but I believe that Babic is very sincere. This is what Stoltenberg has" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to stop for a second. I heard on the French channel that the interpreters were not able to catch up the beginning. So since we need the French translation of the entirety of the portion played, I suggest that we restart the audio tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, did you want us to -- we can do it here -- but do you want us to pause it at some certain points? Might that be more helpful to the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, Mr. Kehoe. I think the procedure is that one of the interpreters reads the transcript and sees whether that is in line with what he hears, and that the other interpreter is then translating, because you never can catch up with the speed of speech. So at the end we wait until the translation is finished. The audio could be restarted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Tudjman's Interpreter: Well you see Belgrade is invoking his assembly, Milosevic says is he controlling. "Tudjman: No, Babic is invoking. "Tudjman's Interpreter: Babic, I'm sorry, is invoking his assembly. Milosevic says he is controlling the generals. And yet he would not receive Babic and talk to him. Belgrade has appointed Mrksic for the commanding officer in Knin, and yet they are sending Novakovic down to Geneva. And all of this again goes to show that we have been again led on. Moreover as Mr. Sarinic just stated, one members of that delegation is Prijic who is the grey eminence of Martic. "Galbraith: I understand the dilemma, but I believe that Babic is very sincere. This is what Stoltenberg has proposed and what I believe that the Serb delegation is prepared to accept. "Tudjman: One from Serb delegation, and another not, and so on, and so on. But we'll see. "Galbraith: Is it true that the operation is scheduled to begin tomorrow morning? "Tudjman: If the negotiation is not satisfied in Geneva, then yes. "Galbraith: Okay. Thank you very much, Mr. President ... Robert Finn. "Tudjman: Finn. "Galbraith: So you may see him when I am out of town. "Zuzul: Mr. President, may I only one sentence. In my talks in Washington, the spirit was the same like the one that Ambassador Galbraith expressed, but neither in one moment it wasn't said that our bilateral relations can be jeopardized. "Galbraith: I think that this is a result of the feeling that there is an genuine opportunity for peace, and that is why I added that point. I want you to know candidly what the situation is."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, turning to this particular comment by Ambassador Galbraith, as you sat there and even today, sir, do you believe that Galbraith's additional warnings about harm to bilateral relations, do you think that accurately reflected the United States' position?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Now when I see all this and even back then, and that's why I intervened, it seemed to me that Mr. Galbraith is adding certain things or interpreting them differently from what was expressed by other representatives of the United States. Here, it is clear that he added a certain tone to this. My interpretation was that Mr. Galbraith, who was and remained my friend, wanted to play a personal role in all that, pushing a peace plan that he had co-authored, but it was my impression then and now that he wasn't succeeding in presenting this peace plan successfully, not even in Washington.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And is the peace plan that you referring to the Z-4 plan?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Correct. That was the Z-4 plan. Your Honour, at this time, we'd like to offer into evidence 65 ter 1D2719.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1491.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1491 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would like to turn our attention to D1454 which is a transcript of the VONS meeting. And this VONS meeting took place directly after the meeting with Ambassador Galbraith, did it not?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Correct. I'm sorry, I think that between the meeting and the beginning of VONS, he was received. I think that -- he was received in Washington. I think that was between the two meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me one second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I may the English correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that is what Mr. Misetic was just telling me, that there has been some mistake, so if we could have some clarification on that score.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would please, well, approximately the witness himself has identified a translation issue. Could you explain to us what is not reflecting what you said in Croatian in the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said in Croatian that, to the best of my recollection, President Tudjman received an invitation from Geneva, where our negotiating team was supposed to negotiate with the Serbs, and he was informed -- he received a call saying that those negotiations had fallen through. I think that call was after our meeting with Galbraith and before the meeting of VONS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification, Mr. Ambassador. As you can see this the -- the cover page of this VONS meeting from the 3rd of August, beginning at 1800 hours. You, of course, can see your name on there as the last one. I trust it is in alphabetical order. It is. And if we can move to page 3 in the English of this document which -- and just address the particular point that you just made concerning a call from Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I would address the point that you just made right after the meeting that we not be outplayed. It notes: "Pasalic just called me five minutes ago from Geneva and told me that the Serbs did not want to consent to our proposals." I can see that in the English. Can you see that, Mr. Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Staying with that particular item, based on your dealings with President Tudjman, the VONS, and as a diplomat of many years, and you note that in paragraph 19 that -- the last sentence that President Tudjman always gave priority to a peaceful solution if there was a minimum prospect of the same. You also note above that: "If the Serb decision had agreed to the Croatian demands on 3 August, peace negotiations would have started and reintegration of all occupied areas would have been carried out." Consistent with that, after this phone call, you are the first person who was called to talk at this meeting after a series of comments by the president. And I address you to -- it would be page 4 and 5 in the English. I believe it is the same in the Croatian. You were called upon to talk by President Tudjman. Now, when you were in Washington, had you received a call from President Tudjman to come back and talk to VONS?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Correct. The president talked to me, asked me when I was coming, and if I remember correctly, he asked me to come as soon as possible, because just after my arrival, a VONS meeting was supposed to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, based on -- on your experience and going back to some of the strategic goals that you had talked about previously concerning using diplomacy, why do you think -- why do you think Ambassador -- Tudjman turned to you and then to Minister Granic first to talk about the international assessment of this? Why?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: It is my opinion that Tudjman, at that time of making an important decision considered all the three strategic goals of Croatia. He was aware of the reports that Granic and I were about to give him. But he wanted that everyone should take into account the positions of the international community and the relations of Croatia with the international community at that time of making an important decision. Tudjman never improvised anything at such moments. It is obvious that he placed great weight on Croatia's relations with the world, and he wanted us to consider that carefully before moving on to other aspects of a possible decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in page 5 of this transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- you continue to talk and you lay out the conditions that the United States has set forth for you in your discussions with Holbrooke and Leon Firth. In the centre of that page you note: "However, the second point is that attention should be paid to the civilians and what will happen to them. All the more so, because that was mentioned a number of times, the closer we came to the end of the [sic] talks." Once again, Mr. Ambassador, based on your experience with President Tudjman, would he have taken that admonition from you very seriously before agreeing to the execution of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Quite certainly he would have taken that into account. As you see, I emphasise certain points that I had heard in Washington and elsewhere, but primarily in Washington. But what is more important, Mr. Tudjman knew what I was about to say, because I had already told him. He wanted me to emphasise those points so that all the others should hear them and take them into account, all those who were about to take part in making the decision, but also implementing that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it would be at this juncture that I would ask the assistance of the Ambassador in discussing the comments in the Brioni transcript, because as you understand this is a logical place to get an interpretation based on his experience with President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered the matter, and Mr. Kehoe, during the break, and the Chamber came to the conclusion that we'd like to hear from the witness what he personally experienced as far as the use of language is concerned in his meetings with -- with President Tudjman. But, on the other hand, that the Chamber -- that is -- will not be assisted but then hearing from the witness how he interprets what was said at a meeting he did not attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will say in response to that, Mr. President, that -- and I accept the admonition, I just want to put what I say on the record. Obviously, the cross-examination we saw for most of Friday was an interpretation called upon by the OTP concerning issues that Ms. Skare Ozbolt was not in. I would say with regard to this particular -- if Your Honours want to dispense with down the line as being of no consequence, I would ask the Court to at least hear at this point because it has to do with the various adjective/verb usage here and the usage of the operative word by the president --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we would not mind. I think I earlier used already the word exegesis as not something that the Chamber would like to focus on. And that was totally apart from what we heard from this witness. Ms. Gustafson, you'd like to --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just respond to the one point about comparing this to the cross-examination on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That was a completely different context. The purpose of putting those transcripts to the witness was for impeachment primarily, and the fact that she was there was -- either went to -- it was either for impeachment or to show that she had a lack of knowledge about what was at those meetings. It is a different context than what is going on here on direct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, it is consistent with this question of how a Tudjman associate and person that worked with him would have interpreted this comment. Those are the questions that were asked. And than would simply be the question asked of Ambassador Zuzul. If you heard this, how would you interpret it? And that is relevant and significant, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think it was in response to answers given by the witness about -- the knowledge of the witness about the way of thinking, of, if I could summarize it that way, it's not a very accurate summary of President Tudjman or his approaches. And, of course, in cross-examination that makes a difference. I would not disallow. But I said the Chamber thinks it will not be assisted by it. If there will be a short question on that and a short answer, then -- but what the Chamber wants to avoid, and that's again, is not limited -- is not specially focussing on this witness.
