I earlier said we should avoid that everyone who comes in and knows or has seen Mr. Tudjman on television starts explaining what -- without knowing the whole of the context of it, without knowing all of the other evidence that this Chamber received so that we are overloaded with five, ten, or fifteen different interpretations of what people think he may have meant. And the Chamber would like you then to focus -- and that's the issue. You said would -- could specifically add to what others might say about this is the use of a certain word.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- that's, as I said before, that certainly adds. But no lengthy because this happened a half year ago, three months ago, this, therefore we have to understand this language in such and such a way, that is not really what will assist the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It will be two minutes, Mr. President. I would like to show you this one line, Ambassador Zuzul in P461. It is page 29 in the English and page 55 in the B/C/S. And I understand this is the Brioni meeting that you were not in attendance. In the second insertion down concerning -- directing to the president's comments, Ambassador Zuzul, it notes that a leaflet of this sort, general chaos, the victory of the Croatian army supported by the international community and so forth. Serbs you already withdrawing and so forth, and we are appealing to you not to withdraw. We guarantee ... The way it's been interpreted in this exhibit is this means giving them a way out while pretending to guarantee civil rights, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi is on his feet, therefore I would like to instruct the witness to wait to answer the question once Mr. Kehoe has finished it. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm just suggesting to the witness to read the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think it is on the screen, sir. I would suggest that we read the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in our discussions, Mr. Ambassador, in reading the B/C/S version you have a different interpretation of that line by President Tudjman. And I believe you said that you heard that line -- that word used before, once significant word. Briefly can you explain this to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Sorry, I might have not been clear. That the witness reads the B/C/S, so we get an interpretation from the booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If that is satisfactory, if you can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it is a first start. It will not be the final resolution of either a transcript issue or a translation issue, but we could invite the witness to read it aloud and then -- Could you please read the relevance -- relevant line; that is, the last line of the intervention by the president, starting with a leaflet of this sort, that's the beginning of the paragraph, the intervention. Could you read the last line after the dots.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "That means give them a route in that way, while ostensibly guaranteeing their civil rights, et cetera."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the particular word that was used in that fashion, do you see the English translation, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: I see two different translations of that particular word, which does not surprise me. The translation in the transcript of this meeting is different from the translation given from the booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... answer the question that was put to by Mr. Kehoe. The Chamber will, as we earlier said, will pay very precise attention to any transcription or any translation issue. So if you could please answer Mr. Kehoe's question. Perhaps you can briefly repeat what you asked the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I asked you, and then that particular word was used in that fashion, do you see it in the English interpretation? And I'm asking you how you interpreted it, how you interpret that word?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President, although I'm not a linguistic expert, I do know the Croatian language well, and I have a relatively good knowledge of the English language, and I knew Mr. Tudjman very well. I dare to say that the way the word "toboze" was translated in writing does not correspond even lexically, and it certainly doesn't correspond to the way in which Mr. Tudjman used this word. If you allow me to explain, Mr. President, the word "toboze" or "tobozni" is used infrequently in the Croatian language. I know few people who would use it in common speech. However, President Tudjman used the word rather often in various situations. The most common situation where he would use it, this word "toboze," or "tobozni," would be when he spoke about certain ideas that he was aware of but was not fully convinced or fully confident about them. And oftentimes, as I believe you can find in documents, he would say freedom of the press; he would say, toboze, freedom of the press; civil rights, he would say, toboze, civil rights. And a number of such examples exist. From what I know, he took a distance, speaking from the viewpoint of the previous system in which we used to live, and if you allow me to say one more thing. I think it is completely wrong to translate "toboze," which is an adjective in Croatian, to translate it as an active verb, pretending to. You can't translate it that way. It can be translated in various ways, but not as a verb in active form. I believe you are able to check that with better experts than I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are invited to give your comments, so tell us what would be the right thing, the right translation. How you understand the line. This would be done in two minutes from what I understood from Mr. Kehoe. But there's no need at this moment to say what others did wrong. The Chamber will, as I said before, will pay thorough attention to the matter, so just tell us what your understanding of this line would be.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the simplest way would be, in view of the limitations of my knowledge of English, for me to say how I understand it in English: "[In English] Guarantee so-called human rights or civil rights." [Interpretation] And I believe that gives different meaning to this sentence. If you use in English "to pretend," then the English version would be guaranteeing pretended human rights, which would be a passive form of the same meaning. But it doesn't mean we will pretend to guarantee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can move back to D454 [sic] which is the VONS meeting and go back where we left off. And if we could turn to page 8 of the English at the insertion of Mr. Granic being asked to speak. This is at D1454. [Microphone not activated] As we're waiting for the B/C/S version to come up, I know that you can speak English, Mr. Ambassador. But it -- it's a translation of -- the president says: "Who would like to take the floor next? Mate, please." And then Dr. Granic begins to speak. He is the foreign minister. And he talks about having talks with Kinkel and van den Broek. And who are those two individuals, Kinkel and van den Broek?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Mr. Kinkel was the German minister of foreign affairs at the time. Mr. van den Broek was at a certain point in time the Dutch minister of foreign affairs. However, at that point in time I believe he was the representative of the European Commission. He performed several international duties which led him to be in contact with the developments in former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we move down to the next paragraph. And why did -- based on your diplomatic experience would the president want to hear what Dr. Granic has to say in his discussions with Mr. Kinkel and Mr. van den Broek?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Well, evidently the president wanted to have the whole international picture or, rather, what the international situation would be in case Croatia should opt for such a military operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we move down to the next paragraph, Mr. Granic says: "None of them said anything to the contrary as far as any possible military action on our part is concerned. They only warned that we should be careful." Do you say that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, as we move through this, Ambassador, the president asked if anybody was going to dissent, did he not? Did he not ask the people in the VONS meeting whether or not they would agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: I don't know how he formulated the question, but he did ask if everybody agreed with the decision to launch a military action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And given this discrepancy that has been put forth in this translation as opposed to your report about cautioning civilians, when you look at this picture, sir, and you are here today, I ask you, would President Tudjman have wanted military -- Operation Storm planned in a way that violated the conditions set forth by the United States or the international community?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: I am deeply convinced that he would not have. He -- or, rather, President Tudjman wanted the operation to be carried and he believed that it would be carried out in a way that would only reinforce the support of the international community and the consideration it showed. I would like to note that we here -- here see only snippets of the situation. However, President Tudjman at all times and everywhere kept in mind the fact that there was another part of the Croatian that was occupied, namely, Eastern Slavonia and Baranja. I heard this from him oftentimes, and we negotiated this matter with the international community on several occasion, and that was that he could resolve the reintegration of that part of territory only through cooperation with the United States of America. Based on this and based on my other dealings with President Tudjman, I am personally convinced that he would not have made a decision which would be contrary to the clear messages we received from Washington and, as you can see from this document, from other amicable countries as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me be very direct with you, Mr. Ambassador, concerning certain of the allegations that have come forward in this case. During all of your meetings, all of your discussions with President Tudjman and other leaders of the Republic of Croatia, did you ever hear any discussion where it was planned to drive the Serb population out of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Discussions which would have aimed at planning the expulsion of the civilian population were not something I was ever part of, nor was I aware of such discussions ever having taken place. I, or the majority of the individuals who were the top leadership of Croatia at the time and who had expertise, would have agreed to something like that. Let me be precise. I never heard from President Tudjman anything of the sort, and I never received any instructions from him that would have led to the expulsion of the civilian population from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, just to avoid whatever confusion, you said: "I or the majority of the individuals were the top leadership of Croatia at the time and who had expertise would have agreed to something like that." May I take it that if you were referring to planning of the expulsion of Serbs that you intended to say: Would not have agreed to something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Mr. President. Thank you for your interpretation, because I may have speeded up too much now, and the sentence was given an erroneous meeting -- meaning. What I wanted to say that was VONS was composed of a number of experts, intellectuals --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wanted to put on the record that there was an apparent mistake by whomever. I did not make a new translation of your words. I just tried to understand them. I have understood them by now. Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, with concern to information coming back on burning and looting, did you ever hear any approval, agreement, to -- by the authorities of the Republic of Croatia to allow looting and burning to take place in the Krajina after Operation Storm as a way to drive out the Serbs and to keep them out.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: I heard concerns, but I never heard any approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And tell us about what the concerns were.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Since I primarily communicated with the international community, I can say, to the best of my recollection, that in the immediate aftermath of Operation Storm, I never learnt that the international community or anyone else should have information to the effect that these events took place on a mass scale. That was not the sort of information I had. Quite the contrary. There was an intervention on the part of Ambassador Galbraith, when he joined a group of departing Serbs, possibly in an attempt to prevent any adverse effects it may have. I invited Ambassador Galbraith, and he was accompanied by an entire high-level US delegation, to the place where I grew up to attend a large public event. My intention was for him to simply see what sort of a reaction the simple folk would have upon seeing him and the American delegation and that nobody would perceive his calls for the protection of the civilians in a negative way. As a matter of fact, President Tudjman knew that they were invited and in fact attended this particular celebratory event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us move ahead to some of the negotiations from post-Operation Storm and directing your attention to paragraph 24 concerning the diplomatic efforts for Eastern Slavonia. And I'd like to draw your attention to some comments concerning a -- P449. But before we do that, and as that is coming up on the screen, when the reports of these looting and burning was taking place, Ambassador, you know, were there concerns inside the Croatian government, and what were they?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: I already said that I was aware of these concerns, and I discussed these matters with Minister Granic in particular. Both of us told the president that we should keep in mind the reactions of the international community, since that was our duty. I can tell you now that President Tudjman, too, was concerned over that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, whenever the word concern is used, do you have any concerns that could, from my understanding of the English language, mean two things? Concern about this to happen, or concern about this happening. Could we always try to clearly identify which of the two we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, taking the lead from the President and talking about these concerns, can we talk about these concerns in the two capacities that the president just highlighted. Concern that it was happening -- concern that it was in fact happening and concern about this to happen. I mean, those two issues. Can you explain what the concern was coming from not only you and Dr. Granic but President Tudjman? And if you could include in that the potential impact on international relations with entities such as the United States.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: I think that we can use the term "concern" to denote both meanings, the concern about what was happening and the concern about the impact it might have that was undesirable for everyone, including President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Make that more concrete. I mean, you talked about -- apparently you agree that on a factual basis where I was making the distinction, of course, on the basis of a theoretical distinction, could you tell us what you learned about the concerns, expressed about burning and looting to take place and what you learned or what you observed about concerns or even experienced yourself about looting and burning occurring within a concrete way, rather than in an abstract way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Neither then nor now can I claim that I knew specifically what was happening in the field. To put it candidly, it was not my duty to inform the president about something I know little of. However, as reactions from the international community started coming in, and that was, unless I'm mistaken, sometime in late August, these were warnings to the effect that should events that are unacceptable continue to happen in the field, it might affect the relations we had with the United States. At some point, I don't recall when exactly, I discussed the matter with -- with the president, and it was my impression - I emphasise it was my impression - that he was concerned about what was happening in field. It was also my impression - and this is something we discussed at greater length - that it concerned him in relation to how this might affect our future relations with the international community, since, at that point in time, President Tudjman wanted to seize the point of victory, in the subsequent negotiations. That's how I perceived his position. He didn't want the situation in the field to threaten the attainment of our goals at a point in time which he perceived as a good negotiating position for the fate of Eastern Slavonia and Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, based on your discussions with him, if there was some alienation of relations with the United States, did he believe that that would have affected the negotiations on the peaceful reintegration of Eastern Slavonia that you discuss in paragraph 24?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: At the time President Tudjman firmly believed that we accepted the position expressed by the United States that they would assist us in finding a settlement of the problem in Eastern Slavonia and Baranja. I discussed this point with him extensively. Unlike others in Croatia, he was certain that this reintegration could take place only through peaceful and not military means. He was definitely aware of the fact that he should not in any way risk or threaten to undermine this position held by the United States at the time [In English] unlike others in Croatia but unlike some, or some others in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So that would be line 14, you would say, unlike some others in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go to another subject which is the post-Operation Storm negotiations that you begin to discuss in paragraph 24. And on the screen, we have before us a meeting, the 18th of August, 1995, with Ambassadors Holbrooke, General Clark, and Ambassador Galbraith.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if can I turn to page 7 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I might add I have been informed that they have updated this translation, and that it should be page 4. Now, Mr. Ambassador, you are present at this discussion, are you not? And --

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I have also been informed it is page 31 in the B/C/S. And if we can just review going to the middle of that wage which is: "I understand." Ambassador Holbrooke says: "I understand. I would like to be very honest because our administration has been giving you different signals about military activity in the past month." When you heard that, Mr. Ambassador, what did you interpret that to mean? What did you think he was talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: It was my impression that he referred to the channel of communication that went through Ambassador Galbraith at times, through Ambassador Holbrooke at times, and through me. I think he referred to something that we discussed earlier on; namely, certain messages which were not identical at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continuing on: "In November we asked you not to attack, and you did not. In March I flew over here and we agreed, and then you and Gore announced it in Copenhagen, and you did not attack." What are we talking about there, Mr. Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Well, by way of General interpretation, this refers to what I pointed out on a number of occasions. Every time the position of the international community, or specifically of the United States of America, was that we should not launch a military operation. And if that position was expressed in such a way that it was believed that such a military operation would threaten our good relations, it was followed up on. It was agreed to, and this is something that Ambassador Holbrooke referred to here. In fact he referred to two very important meetings where, as I frequently point out, discussions were held with the United States about the issue of Eastern Slavonia. Regardless of the other matters that we discussed as well, I said that President Tudjman always kept in mind the issue of the reintegration of Eastern Slavonia and Baranja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe. Could I just briefly inquire with you, Mr. Waespi, the issue of no attack if there would be a signal of the United States not to attack, is that a matter in dispute?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I don't think it's in dispute, but there was quite some back and forth with Ambassador Galbraith on green light, yellow and red light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is another matter. That is anther matter, what they said. But we have dealt with the issue whether there would have been an attack, if there would be a clear signal, do not attack. My question is whether that is in dispute. Not to say what -- what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I would love to consider it over the break and [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you see the distinction I make. Between whether there was such a signal is a different matter, might well have been no signal or an ambiguous signal. I'm just asking about whether the position taken apparently by Mr. Kehoe, and at least which appears from his questioning, that if there would have been a signal, you should not attack, coming from the United States, whether nevertheless, it was the intention of President Tudjman or whether it could be feasible that there would nevertheless be an attack. That's the issue. Then we will hear from you after the break. Mr. Kehoe, shall we give Mr. Waespi immediately time to -- or at --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Absolutely Judge. If we could take his issue off the table, I would be very happy. I go back to addressing this because of Mt. Tieger -- as a matter of fact, Judge, you asked the same question of Mr. Tieger, and he got the result which gave an answer which causes me to go through this. So if we're taking that off the table, I will be -- I will move ahead. I will be very content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will have to verify whether I put exactly the same question to him, but I will --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, that might be of some importance. Mr. Zuzul, we have another break. We will resume at ten minutes to 1.00. And could I already inquire with the parties about time needed for cross as matters stand now? Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think one session, certainly, and perhaps a bit more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I anticipate either about 15 minutes or nothing at all, and I will certainly let you know at the end of the session today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Roughly the same, Your Honour. And I probably won't let you know a the end of today but tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that we -- yes. Then we resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ambassador Zuzul, just staying on this page in the English towards the bottom, and I believe it is the next page, page 32 in the B/C/S, there's a comment by Ambassador Holbrooke that I would like to direct you to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can scroll that down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On that page, Mr. Ambassador, at the bottom of the English, Ambassador Holbrooke says: "As you know, we were publicly saying we were concerned, but privately you knew what we wanted." Now going back to your statement, I just would like to point out some things in your statement and ask some general questions. You are had noted for us previously, and you also note in paragraph 24 that President Tudjman wanted the -- insisted on the involvement of the United States in the negotiations for Eastern Slavonia. I would like to -- by the way, were those negotiations successful, ultimately with the assistance of the United States?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Those negotiations were very successful. They concerned the peaceful reintegration of Eastern Slavonia. And that was one of the rare, complete successes of the international community in resolving the crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would like to broaden the question out a bit and take it from Ambassador Holbrooke's statement and talk about the wider conflict in Bosnia as Croatia began to move through Bosnia with the Bosnian Muslims and the HVO. Did the United States continue to stay involved? And did the president and others in the government continue to meet with the United States to get their assistance and guidance through the rest of the fighting prior to Dayton?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: This communication prior to the Dayton Accords continued at various levels all the time. I think it was carried out very well, and I think it was very important to the preparation of the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And just summing up, in paragraph 24 you talk about the operations after the Split Agreement, Summer 95, Operation Storm, Operation Maestral, and Operation Southern Move. Do you see that reference, sir. It's in paragraph 26, I said 25, I meant 26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I think you said 24, but we have now the whole range of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... It's 26, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you say in here that General Gotovina played a crucial role in these operations. Do you know that he was, throughout all of these operations, the operational commander and in charge of the joint HV/HVO forces?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: I cannot claim that I have accurate information about it, but what I knew and what I heard as a diplomat was precisely as you say, that he was in charge of that, and that he was extremely important in all these operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In these operations and when you ultimately went to Dayton, and you do refer to this to some degree, in paragraph 27, did any of the peace negotiation -- negotiators, either prior to Dayton or during Dayton, did they every express their thoughts to about the work done by General Gotovina and the armed forces in bringing about the defeat of the Bosnian Serbs? Did they ever mention that to you, and what were their thoughts?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: All that I heard at that time about General Gotovina were praises for his military capabilities and his abilities in conducting military operations. I really can't remember hearing anything at the time that would run counter to that assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And -- paragraph 27, this is one last question, you say that the Split Agreement, Summer 95, Storm, were not only responsibile for the liberation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, initiation of the peace process in Dayton, but also thanks to these military operations, the conditions were created to reintegrate Eastern Slavonia peacefully without a single drop of blood spilled. Would you add to that Operations Maestral an Operation Southern Move as a intricate part of the whole formula to bring about peace in Dayton?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: Certainly. I was not the only one who said that. All the analysts who spoke about Dayton agreed that one of the premises for Dayton's success was the military victory of the Croatian forces, the HVO and the Bosniak army and the definitive defeat of the Serbian aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, thank you very much. Mr. President, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. You have joined with other Defence teams in beating the clock. Mr Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will beat the clock even more, Your Honour. I don't have any questions for the witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Beat the clock or you don't beat it, more or less. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... Your Honour, I have no clock, so I don't have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Waespi, are you ready to start your cross-examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would actually prefer to start tomorrow morning if that is possible. I'm a little bit surprised that the Defence didn't take the whole session today. I -- I could start, of course, if ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps let's try to use our time. It will not be dramatic because I foresee that there will be some gaps perhaps later this week, especially on Thursday, but, at the same time, I'll -- let me just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, you're invited to start. I already announce that I have a decision to deliver and which I will do at the end of this session. It's a relatively short one, so you have approximately half an hour. The Chamber never knows what happens. The next witness could have a headache tomorrow. Everything is possible. Therefore, let's use our time to moment that we have it. But, again, I not push you too hard. Half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ambassador. I'm sure you experience with this cross-examination will be less painful than the hard-talk cross-examination you had with Mr. Sebastian a couple of years ago. Let me start with a point you made in your witness statement that was at paragraph 23. This is now D1485. And that deals with the warnings or conditions you say the Americans put you in relation to the attack of Operation Storm. Now in paragraph 23, it says that towards the end of the paragraph: "Moreover, the necessity to protect the Serb civilian population was specifically emphasised at the meetings. We, from diplomacy constantly warned that the international community was going to pay the highest attention to this, and I can testify to the fact that President Tudjman truly respected this." Now, in the previous sentence, the meetings that you talked about, was that the VONS meeting of the 3rd of August, 1995, where these concerns about the protection of the Serb civilian population was emphasised?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: No. What I referred to in paragraph 23 concerned the period afterwards, not just after the VONS meeting. To be precise, at the VONS meeting, I presented the views of the international community. These concerns -- this concern relates to a more permanent state of affairs, where we conveyed what the international community was thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And by "we," you mean whom?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: In this context, when I say "we," I mean Mr. Granic, who was the foreign minister; Mr. Sanader who was then deputy foreign minister; several ambassadors, who had direct communication. Not only myself but the ambassador to Brussels as well. All those people who were in a position to have direct communication either international organisations or with host countries on one hand, and the Croatian government on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. I understand now. So these were concerns that were expressed by the internationals at meetings with you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL
utterances.text: I'm not sure it is exactly what you say. I think it is exactly as I wrote here. At meetings with representatives of the international community, the necessity was emphasised to protect civilians. And we cautioned the government and President Tudjman in our talks with the government, that the international community would be paying special attention to this, and I believe that both the government and President Tudjman took this into consideration, and it was my belief that if things would happen contrary to the wishes of the international community, then the steps taken by the international community would not agree with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. Let me move on to a different issue; that is, what you testified about Bihac. Now, it's true, is it not - and we can get P461, page 1, on the screen - that President Tudjman told everybody during that meeting in Brioni that there was no more pretext given by the situation in Bihac to go ahead, because the situation in Bihac actually relaxed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I think you're asking the witness what President Tudjman told everybody during a meeting where the witness was not present and where the Chamber has expressed its concerns about asking to interpret what was said at that meeting. That's the situation I find myself in at this moment receiving the evidence. Is that really what you intended to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I believe the witness testified that -- and maybe we can go back to Exhibit P458.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you were asking him what President Tudjman told everyone during that meeting and, at the same time, presenting to him the text of what he said. A meeting where he was not present. Do you really think that it would add to the information in a meaningful way? I'm not saying that the subject, as such, should not be touched upon. I'm just saying something about the way in which you're doing it. I would -- if I -- I have never been at the Brioni meeting. If someone would give me the text and say, This is what was said at the Brioni meeting, and then ask me, Is it true that they said this and this? Then I would say, If the transcript is correct, yes; If the transcript is not correct, no. I mean, what else, what does it add?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Because I believe the witness testified earlier that the -- can I have a moment, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not saying that you could not touch upon the Bihac and whether that what role they played, and whether that was the same at 3rd of August, after the 3rd of August, before the 3rd of August. utterances.text: Then the Chamber decides that you will be -- that you will continue your cross-examination tomorrow. Mr. Zuzul, you see, a courtroom is part of life. I will invite Madam Usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which gives us time to deliver a decision. It's not actually a decision but reasons for a decision, because these are the Chamber's reasons for its decision on protective measures for Witness 13. On the 12th of February, 2009, the Prosecution requested the protective measures of testimony in closed session and pseudonym for Witness 13. On the 23rd of February, the Cermak Defence responded that it opposed the Prosecution's request. On the same day, both the Gotovina Defence and the Markac Defence joined this response. On the 24th of February, 2009, the Chamber granted the Prosecution's request, with reasons to follow. As the Chamber has held in previous decisions on protective measures, the party seeking protective measures for a witness must demonstrate an objectively grounded risk to the security or welfare of the witness or the witness's family, should it become known that the witness has given evidence before the Tribunal. The question of whether to grant protective measures involves a delicate balance between the right of the accused to a public trial, on the one hand; and the interests and need for protection and privacy for victims and witnesses on the other. In this respect, the Chamber is mindful that the granting of protective measures does not negatively affect an accused's other fair trial rights, such as the right to examine witnesses against him. Even though the granting of protective measures is, and should be, the exception to the rule of a public trial, the threshold for when it should be granted cannot be set too high. For example, to exclude persons who have not experienced threats and harassment would defy the purpose of the measures; namely, protection for risks that might occur as a result of the testimony. The Chamber must therefore make a risk assessment, and inherent in such an assessment is applying a certain level of caution and erring on the safe side. The Chamber adds these words as an explanation to the approach it has taken with regard to protective measures in this case in general. Witness 13 expressed concerns about testifying publicly. She is a Serb who does not live permanently in Croatia but returns there regularly from her country of residence. The subject of Witness 13's testimony involves a particular crime incident allegedly involving a number of Croatian soldiers, and it took place in the area where the witness lives when she is in Croatia. On one occasion, when the witness was temporarily back in Croatia, a uniformed police officer and one man in civilian clothes visited her and asked about her experiences in 1995 and about one of the accused. According to the witness, that same police officer came back some weeks later, but, on this occasion, the witness was too afraid to talk to him. These events left the witness fearful of testifying. For the aforementioned reasons, and bearing in mind the general considerations mentioned earlier, the Chamber found that the Prosecution had demonstrated an objectively grounded risk to the security of Witness 13, should it become known that she has given evidence before the Tribunal. The Chamber considered, that, in light of the nature of the anticipated evidence of this witness, any protective measures, short of testimony in closed session, would be insufficient. For these reasons, the Chamber granted the motion for protective measures for Witness 13. And this concludes the Chamber's reasons for its decision to grant protective measures for Witness 13. We adjourn for the day. We will resume tomorrow, the 9th of June, 9.00, Courtroom III.
